title: Listen and take notes: stage 1 of a case interview
description: Everything later links back to the goal you write down now. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: The case starts before you say a word. How you listen and what you write down in the first minute decides how easy the next thirty will be. Here is what to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
body:
Stage 1 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why it matters

Everything later links back to the goal you write down now.

The common mistake

Nodding along when you don’t understand, then getting lost ten minutes later.

What to do, and what to say

Listen and note

Shorthand notes on the left of your page. Write the client’s goal at the top, in a box, with its number and deadline.

"Thank you for the case, this is an interesting problem."

Don’t fake understanding

If a word or number is unclear, mark it in your notes and ask as soon as the interviewer finishes the prompt. Never build on something you didn’t understand.

"Before I recap, one quick check: when you said X, did you mean...?"

Draw early insights

React to interesting facts as they land. It shows commercial instinct and flags a branch to revisit.

"Interesting that revenue fell while volume held. I may want to come back to pricing."

Practise the moment

Read the situation and say your answer out loud before you open the model.

The interviewer has just finished reading the prompt to you. What do you say first?

Show a strong answer

"Thank you for the case, this is an interesting problem." Then write the goal at the top of your page.

Why it works: A calm, warm opening buys you a second and sets the tone of a conversation between colleagues.

Mid-prompt, the interviewer says "the client’s contribution has fallen" and you’re not sure what they mean by contribution.

Show a strong answer

Mark it in your notes, let them finish, then: "Before I recap, one quick check: when you said contribution, did you mean contribution margin per unit?"

Why it works: Asking at the end of the prompt is polite, and far cheaper than building on a misunderstanding.

You hear: "volumes are stable but revenue is down 8%". React out loud.

Show a strong answer

"Interesting that revenue fell while volume held. That points to price or mix, so I may want to come back to that."

Why it works: Spotting implications as facts land shows commercial instinct.

Next stage: recap.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. All ten stages, with every phrase, are on the free perfect casing page.
